# IFN-γ-resistant CD28 CAR-T cells demonstrate increased survival, efficacy, and durability in multiple murine tumor models

**Authors:** Stefanie R. Bailey; Hana N. Takei; Giulia Escobar; Michael C. Kann; Amanda A. Bouffard; Tamina Kienka; Valentina M. Supper; Alexander Armstrong; Diego Salas-Benito; Merle K. Phillips; Filippo Birocchi; Sonika Vatsa; Harrison Silva; Irene Scarfò; Marc Wehrli; Korneel Grauwet; Eli P. Darnell; Charlotte E. Graham; Mark B. Leick; Felix Korell; Trisha R. Berger; Marcela V. Maus

## Abstract

Interferon-γ (IFN γ) plays complex and occasionally contradictory roles in cancer, which can impact patient responses to treatments such as immunotherapies. We recently demonstrated that IFNγ production by chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells is not required for efficacy in hematologic tumor models, whereas IFNγ receptor signaling in solid tumor cells facilitated CAR-T cell adhesion and antigen-specific cytotoxicity. Here, we show that IFNγ induces apoptosis of CAR-T cells bearing a CD28 intracellular signaling domain, which can be reduced through targeting of IFNγ or IFNγ receptor (IFNγR). In hematologic malignancies, knockout of IFNγ receptor (IFNγRKO) in CAR-T cells increased their persistence without compromising efficacy. In xenograft and syngeneic solid tumor models, IFNγR knockout CAR-T cells displayed more potent tumor control, prolonged survival, and improved T cell memory that conferred protection from tumor rechallenge. RNA sequencing of tumor-infiltrating IFNγRKO CAR-T cells derived from tumor-bearing mice revealed increased cell death in tumor cells. Collectively, these data show that inhibition of IFNγ signaling can increase the expansion and anti-tumor activity of CD28-based CAR-T cells in liquid and solid tumors.

## Abstract

IFNγ-resistant CD28 CAR-T cells exhibit potent anti-tumor activity due to reduced cell death, increased expansion, and long-term memory formation.

## INTRODUCTION

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells have transformed the treatment of patients with hematologic malignancies, with multiple recent approvals for the treatment of B-cell lymphomas, B-cell leukemias, and multiple myeloma. However, one clinical challenge in this setting is the incidence of relapse, which, broadly, can occur through antigen escape of the tumor or insufficient CAR-T cell engraftment and persistence. Evidence suggests that the peak expansion and duration of persistence of CAR-T cells correlates with durable responses in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), and various forms of B cell lymphoma (1–5). Despite limited data from patients with solid tumors who have received CAR-T cells, prior work has shown that higher expansion of CAR-T cells was associated with improved response in patients with gastrointestinal tumors (6). Furthermore, CAR-T cell persistence beyond 6 weeks correlated with superior outcomes in neuroblastoma patients (7). These data highlight the importance of enhanced CAR-T cell expansion and persistence post-infusion to promote therapeutic efficacy.

Interferon-γ (IFNγ) is a proinflammatory cytokine primarily released by T cells and natural killer (NK) cells that activates innate immune cells (8, 9), upregulates immune checkpoint proteins such as programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) on cancer cells and immune cells (10, 11), and can drive target cell death (12–14). IFNγ uptake by T cells increases their cytotoxicity (15), restricts memory formation in response to weak T cell receptor (TCR) activation (16), and drives activation-induced cell death (17). IFNγ receptor (IFNγR) signaling in tumor cells is critical for the success of immune checkpoint blockades (ICBs), such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab, based on retrospective studies identifying IFNG and IFNγ-responsive genes as predictors of ICB response in patients with metastatic melanoma (18) or non-small cell lung cancer (19). Conversely, IFNγ can lead to reduced ICB efficacy due to immune cell death (20) and disruption of intratumoral stem-like T cells (21). Given the potent production of IFNγ by CAR-T cells following infusion, we sought to better understand the role of this cytokine and its receptor in mediating both toxicities and anti-tumor effects in hematologic malignancies and solid tumors.

We have previously reported that pharmacologic or genetic targeting of IFNγ production by CAR-T cells did not affect efficacy against hematologic malignancies and could potentially mitigate cytokine release syndrome by reducing downstream monocyte and macrophage activation (22). Further, we observed that IFNγ knockout in CAR-T cells with a CD28 costimulatory domain led to their increased expansion following antigen exposure in vitro, suggesting that IFNγ may limit CAR-T cell responses. However, IFNγ-deficient CAR-T cells were shown to exhibit reduced cytotoxicity against solid tumors (22). A separate study indicated that stimulation of IFNγR upregulated adhesion molecules on solid tumor cells critical for achieving sufficient avidity for CAR-T cell cytotoxicity (23). Based on these findings, we hypothesized that selectively reducing IFNγ receptor signaling in CAR-T cells—rather than eliminating IFNγ itself—would enhance CAR-T cell survival and persistence. At the same time, maintaining IFNγ engagement with its receptor on solid tumor cells would increase tumor susceptibility to CAR-T cell-mediated killing.

## RESULTS

### Knockout of IFNγ or IFNγ receptor drives greater CD28 CAR-T cell expansion in vitro

We previously reported that the genetic deletion of IFNγ in CD19-targeting CAR-T cells with either a CD28 or 4–1BB costimulatory domain limited potential toxicities without compromising anti-tumor efficacy in hematologic malignancies (22). Furthermore, we identified that IFNγ knockout (IFNγKO) CAR-T cells exhibited greater expansion in response to the CD19+ Nalm6 leukemia cell line in vitro, particularly in CAR-T cells bearing a CD28 costimulatory domain. To better study the effect of IFNγ signaling on these events, we generated CD19-directed, CD28-bearing CAR-T cells with IFNγ or IFNγR knocked out by CRISPR/Cas9. Similar to our previous study (22), the same vectors included guide RNA to knock out the T cell receptor alpha constant (TRAC) locus either alone (referred to as CARCD19) or in combination with the IFNγ (IFNγKO CARCD19) or IFNγR (IFNγRKO CARCD19). This approach introduced CAR expression in our T cells, while also enabling selection and confirmation of successful gene targeting using CD3 (Fig. 1A). These constructs enabled investigation of the various aspects of IFNγ signaling with an array of CAR-T cells capable of (1) producing and responding to IFNγ (CAR; control), (2) IFNγ-deficient, which respond to but don’t produce IFNγ (IFNγKO CAR) and (3) IFNγ-resistant, which produce IFNγ but do not respond to it (IFNγRKO CAR) (fig. S1A).

Following expansion and CD3- selection (fig. S1B to D), the absence of CD3 and IFNγR on the cell surface of knockout CAR-T cells was confirmed compared with untransduced (UTD) T cells (Fig. 1B; fig. S1E,F). The functional loss of IFNγ receptor was confirmed through exposure to recombinant human IFNγ, which resulted in the loss of STAT1 phosphorylation in IFNγRKO CARCD19 (Fig. 1C; fig. S1G,H). Basic phenotyping revealed that IFNγKO CARCD19 and, to a greater extent IFNγRKO CARCD19, had a CD4:CD8 ratio closer to 1:1 compared to control CARCD19, which was closer to 1:2 (Fig. 1D). Exposure of the CAR-T cells to CD19 antigen resulted in similar activation among groups, as measured by CD69 expression (fig. S1I). In agreement with these findings, all conditions exhibited similar cytokine production in response to CD19 antigen, aside from IFNγ in the IFNγ-deficient CAR-T cells, as expected (Fig. 1E; fig. S2A–C). Both IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 cells exhibited greater expansion in response to antigen exposure in the form of Nalm6 and JeKo-1 target cells (Fig. 1F; fig. S3A), or plate-bound CD19 antigen (fig. S3B), suggesting that loss of IFNγ signaling drives expansion of CAR-T cells independent of tumor/-T cell interactions.

We confirmed our findings with a pharmacologic approach by using blocking antibodies against either IFNγ or IFNγR and observed greater expansion of non-CRISPR/Cas9 edited “wildtype” CAR-T cells in response to stimulation by Nalm6 target cells or CD19 antigen alone (fig. S3C). Importantly, the increased expansion of IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 was antigen-dependent as they did not survive or expand in the absence of antigen or IL-2 (fig. S3D,E). To determine if these effects could be more broadly generalized to CAR-T cells, versus only those with a CD28 costimulatory domain, we generated IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CD19-targeted CAR-T cells bearing a 4–1BB costimulatory domain (Fig. 1G,H). In contrast to CD28 CAR-T cells, we discovered that the loss of IFNγ or IFNγR on CAR-T cells with a 4–1BB costimulatory domain did not drive increased T cell expansion in response to tumor cells (Fig. 1I). These data suggest that IFNγ signaling restricts the growth of CD28, but not 4–1BB, CAR-T cells.

### IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 maintain anti-tumor activity against hematologic malignancies and display greater persistence in vivo

To determine if the loss of IFNγ signaling in CAR-T cells impacts their cytotoxic activity, we first measured and confirmed similar granzyme B and perforin expression in control, IFNγKO, and IFNγRKO CARCD19 following exposure to CD19 antigen (fig. S4A,B). In real-time long-term cytotoxicity assays, we observed that the loss of IFNγ signaling did not compromise cytotoxicity against a one-time exposure to CD19+ Nalm6 or JeKo-1 cell lines in vitro (fig. S4C). Furthermore, IFNγ and IFNγR knockout CARCD19 maintained indistinguishable cytotoxic potential following repetitive exposure to Nalm6 cells in vitro (Fig. 2A).

Next, we measured the anti-tumor activity and expansion of control, IFNγKO, and IFNγRKO CARCD19 in vivo using two different xenograft models. NSG mice bearing the mantle cell lymphoma cell line, JeKo-1, were treated with each of these CAR-T cell groups and monitored for tumor burden, survival, and CAR-T cell expansion (Fig. 2B). We found that although there was some donor variability, IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 mediated similar anti-tumor effects (Fig. 2C,D; fig. S4D,E), and survival (Fig. 2E; fig S4F,G) compared to control CARCD19. All mice, regardless of tumor burden, were sacrificed 75 days post-CAR-T cell infusion due to poor body conditions, likely due to graft-versus-host disease. In agreement with our in vitro data, mice receiving IFNγKO or IFNγRKO CARCD19 cells exhibited higher T cell expansion in the blood 14 days after CAR-T cell infusion (Fig. 2F; fig. S4H,I). The anti-tumor effects were also similar in a stress model of lymphoma (fig. S5), with a transient improvement in anti-tumor activity in the absence of IFNγ signaling. We confirmed the anti-tumor effects in a leukemia (Nalm6) xenograft model (fig. S6A–D). Early serum collection confirmed the presence of human IFNγ in mice that received CARCD19 or IFNγRKO CARCD19-treatment, with corresponding absence of IFNγ in IFNγKO CARCD19-treated mice (fig. S6E). Differences in CAR-T cell expansion and persistence could not be determined, as T cells were not detected at later timepoints, likely due to the aggressive nature of this particular stress model. Collectively, these data demonstrate that neither IFNγ deficiency nor resistance in CAR-T cells compromised their anti-tumor efficacy in models of B-cell malignancies, and IFNγ resistance appeared to increase the expansion of CAR-T cells in vivo.

### Abrogation of IFNγ signaling prompts minimal effects on CD19 CAR-T cell differentiation and exhaustion in vitro

To better understand the effects of IFNγ on CAR-T cells, we performed RNA sequencing on in vitro-activated CARCD19, IFNγKO CARCD19, and IFNγRKO CARCD19. Briefly, CAR-T cell subsets were left untreated or activated with plate-bound CD19 antigen overnight prior to transcriptional profiling. Initial observation revealed that all groups had a similar upregulation of highly expressed genes following exposure to CD19 antigen (CCL1, CCL3/L1, CSF2, GZMB, IL3, NFKBIA, TNFRSF9), suggesting that IFNγ does not change the overall biology of antigen activation (fig. S7A). We next confirmed that the loss of IFNγ signaling in IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 could be visualized at the RNA level as shown by reduced interferon-related gene expression (STAT1, TBX21, IL12RB2) following CD19 activation (fig. S7B). As expected, both IFNγKO (fig. S8A) and IFNγRKO (fig. S8B) CARCD19 displayed a decrease in interferon signaling-related genes compared to control CARCD19.

In agreement with the reported roles of IFNγ in T cell differentiation(16), we observed that IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 exhibited a less differentiated profile (lower CD45RO; higher LEF1, TCF7) compared to control CARCD19 (fig. S8C). To determine if these characteristics translated to the protein level, we first assessed the memory phenotype of the different subsets but observed no significant differences in the differentiation of the CAR-T cell subsets using these metrics (fig. S8D,E). Cell type profiling further revealed a possible skewing of IFNγ-deficient and -resistant CARCD19 away from a type 1 phenotype and towards type 2 (fig. S9A,B). Given that IFNγ can influence T cell subsets(24), we predicted that IFNγ and IFNγR knockout CARCD19 might have a higher percentage of CD4+ type 2 helper cells (Th2; CCR4+CCR6-CXCR3-) compared to type 1 cells (Th1; CCR4-CCR6-CXCR3+). However, there were no significant differences in T cell composition between the groups (fig. S9C).

Since IFNγ is also known to influence immune checkpoint expression (11), we next assessed the expression of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (Lag-3), programmed cell death protein 1(PD-1), and T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain 3 (Tim-3) on all CAR-T cell subsets by flow cytometry following overnight activation with plate-bound CD19 antigen (fig. S10A), JeKo-1 (fig. S10B), or Nalm6 (fig. S10C). Despite seeing changes at the RNA level at this time point, protein expression of these markers was not significantly different between groups. Given that these ‘exhaustion’ markers are also tied to T cell activation, these findings were not surprising. To better identify long-term exhaustion, CAR-T cells were repeatedly exposed to irradiated JeKo-1 or Nalm6 cells and monitored over time (fig. S10D,E). Although IFNγ plays a well-known role in the upregulation of immune checkpoint proteins, IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 did not exhibit a marked change in single positive or triple positive (Lag-3+PD-1+Tim-3+) populations. Collectively, these data suggest that although the loss of IFNγ signaling in CAR-T cells could potentially yield a slightly less differentiated and exhausted population, these do not appear to be the dominant drivers of the observed increases in CAR-T cell expansion.

### Deletion of IFNγ or IFNγR protects CD19-directed CAR-T cells from cell death

Since the differentiation and exhaustion profile of IFNγ-deficient and IFNγ-resistant CARCD19 were not significantly different from control CARCD19, we next sought to determine if they differed in their proliferative potential. RNA sequencing revealed a potential proliferative advantage as CDKN1A, JUN, and IL2 were all increased in IFNγKO (left) and IFNγRKO (right) CARCD19 cells compared to control (Fig. 3A). Despite this upregulation, cell trace violet assays revealed that all CAR-T cell groups exhibited similar proliferative capacities in response to CD19 antigen (fig. S11A,B) and Nalm6 target cells (Fig. 3B; fig. S11C).

We next hypothesized that the persistence of IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 in response to antigen exposure could be due to protection from IFNγ-mediated cell death, consistent with known IFNγ biology in activation-induced cell death of T cells (17), as well as its role in both healthy and cancer cell death via various pathways (14, 25–27). We noted a distinct upregulation of cell death-related genes (STAT1, XAF1, FASLG, CASP1, CASP3) in control CARCD19 compared to IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 after antigen stimulation (Fig. 3A). This was further validated through an increased expression of Annexin V and cleaved Caspase 3 in control CARCD19 compared to IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 following exposure to CD19 antigen (Fig. 3C,D). To further confirm cell death in the CAR-T cell population following antigen exposure, we performed live cell imaging to visualize real-time Annexin V expression and observed a reduction in cell death in both IFNγKO (p=0.0603) and IFNγRKO (p=0.0375) CARCD19 populations compared with control CARCD19 (Fig. 3E). Collectively, these data suggest that the enhanced persistence of IFNγ-deficient and -resistant CAR-T cells is likely due to reduced cell death rather than a proliferative advantage.

To confirm that IFNγ signaling alone could trigger these changes, we stimulated IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARCD19 with plate-bound CD19 antigen overnight in the absence or presence of recombinant human IFNγ (rhIFNγ). As expected, the addition of rhIFNγ was sufficient to restore STAT1 gene expression in IFNγKO CARCD19, but not IFNγRKO CARCD19 (Fig. 3F). This was further confirmed as the addition of rhIFNγ yielded an upregulation of interferon-related genes, such as IRF1, IRF9, TBX21, and JAK2 in IFNγKO CARCD19 compared to IFNγRKO CARCD19 (Fig. 3G; left). This also coincided with an upregulation of cell death-related genes (XAF1, ERAP2, PPARA) (Fig. 3G; right). These findings were confirmed with a pharmacologic approach using blocking antibodies to either IFNγ or IFNγR, which also reduced apoptotic cell death as measured by Annexin V over time (Fig. 3H). Overall, these data demonstrate that IFNγ limits CD28 CAR-T cell persistence by promoting T cell death.

### Loss of IFNγ signaling drives greater survival of mesothelin-specific CD28 CAR-T cells

We have previously demonstrated that IFNγ production by CAR-T cells and IFNγR signaling in the tumor cells is required for optimal cytotoxic activity against solid tumors (22, 23). Now, we hypothesized that deletion of IFNγR in CAR-T cells might enhance their survival and anti-tumor activity in solid tumors. We generated a parallel array of control, IFNγ-deficient, and IFNγ-resistant constructs targeting mesothelin, CARMESO, IFNγKO CARMESO, and IFNγRKO CARMESO, and confirmed the loss of CD3, IFNγR, or IFNγ by flow cytometry (Fig. 4A,B; fig. S12A,B). The functional loss of IFNγ signaling in mesothelin-specific CAR-T cells with targeted deletion of IFNγR was confirmed by the loss of pSTAT1 signaling following exposure to rhIFNγ (fig. S12C). Like CD19-targeted CAR-T cells, we observed a similar activation (fig. S12D) and functional profile (fig. S12E–H) among all groups despite a noticeable shift towards a more equal CD4:CD8 ratio in CAR-T cells lacking IFNγ or IFNγR (Fig. 4C).

IFNγRKO CARMESO exhibited greater expansion following exposure to mesothelin antigen, as shown by live imaging analysis (left) and flow cytometry-based bead counts (right) (Fig. 4D). When challenged with a variety of mesothelin+ pancreatic tumor cell lines in vitro, IFNγKO and IFNγRKO CARMESO exhibited greater expansion against Capan-2 (p<0.0251) or BxPC-3 and Capan-2 (p<0.0359, p<0.0391), respectively compared to control CARMESO (fig. S13A–C). In agreement with the CD19-targeting CAR-T cells, absence of IFNγ signaling did not lead to differences in CAR-T cell differentiation (Fig. 4E), expression of immune checkpoint proteins (Fig. 4F), or proliferation (Fig. 4G; fig. S13D–F). Instead, the absence of IFNγ signaling following antigen exposure resulted in reduced CAR-T cell apoptotic death (Fig. 4H). Collectively, these data suggest that blocking IFNγ signaling through deletion of IFNγ, and to a greater extent IFNγR, results in improved CAR-T cell survival regardless of the antigen specificity or histology of the target antigen-expressing cell.

### IFNγRKO CARMESO exhibit greater anti-tumor activity and survival against pancreatic cancer

We first measured and confirmed similar lgranzyme B and perforin expression in CARMESO, IFNγKO CARMESO, and IFNγRKO CARMESO after antigen exposure (Fig. 5A). When challenged with mesothelin+ AsPC-1, BxPC-3, or Capan-2 tumor cells, we observed that whereas IFNγ-deficient CARMESO had diminished anti-tumor activity (confirming our previous studies), IFNγ-resistant CARMESO retained anti-tumor efficacy similar to control CARMESO (Fig. 5B). We hypothesized that although IFNγKO CARMESO would be incapable of clearing tumors in mice, IFNγRKO CARMESO would retain anti-tumor activity and exhibit increased expansion compared to control CARMESO. To test this hypothesis, NSG mice were injected with AsPC-1 tumor cells two weeks prior to treatment and expansion of CAR-T cells was monitored over time (Fig. 5C,D). As expected, mice receiving IFNγKO CARMESO demonstrated reduced tumor control and survival (Fig. 5E,F). Mice receiving IFNγRKO CARMESO displayed longer tumor control and survival compared to both CARMESO and IFNγKO CARMESO. Of note, several mice from the CARMESO group reached poor body conditions quickly following CAR-T treatment. Overall, these data confirm that whereas the production of IFNγ by CAR-T cells is critical for anti-tumor efficacy, the ability of CAR-T cells to take up IFNγ themselves is not required. Furthermore, blocking IFNγ uptake by CAR-T cells enhanced anti-tumor efficacy and prolonged survival.

### Pancreatic tumors from IFNγRKO CARMESO-treated mice exhibit greater interferon signaling and apoptosis

Given that injected CAR-T cells should be recruited to the tumor site, we hypothesized that although T cell persistence in the blood was not significantly different between treatment groups, there could be an increased accumulation of IFNγRKO CARMESO T cells at the tumor site. To address this and identify potential differences between the top two performers, tumor-bearing mice were treated with control CARMESO or IFNγRKO CARMESO and tumors were collected two weeks later for analysis (Fig. 6A). As hypothesized, analysis of the tumor isolate revealed a 2-fold increase in the CAR-T cell population in conjunction with 50% less tumor cells in mice receiving IFNγRKO CARMESO (Fig. 6B; fig. S14A).

To better understand what could be driving this increased CAR-T cell presence, we used fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate mCherry+ CAR-T and GFP+ tumor cells from the tumor isolate and performed RNA sequencing. This analysis revealed that CAR-T cells from both groups had a similar resting profile prior to injection (Fig. 6C; pre-injection; PRE), whereas CAR-T cells retrieved from the tumors of mice given control CARMESO vs IFNγRKO CARMESO exhibited strikingly different transcriptional profiles (Fig. 6C; post-injection; POST). Furthermore, tumor cells collected from mice receiving no treatment (tumor only; TO), control CARMESO, or IFNγRKO CARMESO displayed an overall difference in gene expression (Fig. 6D).

We first explored the CAR-T cell compartment, where some interferon-related genes were upregulated more in IFNγRKO CARMESO, whereas most of the interferon signature was higher in control CARMESO as expected (Fig. 6E). CARMESO and IFNγRKO CARMESO had a similar differentiation in vitro (PRE), whereas IFNγRKO CARMESO retrieved from the tumor (POST) exhibited greater differentiation (higher CD45RO, GZMA, GZMB) but retained expression of the stemness gene CTNNB1 (fig. S14B). There was a broad expression of immune checkpoint proteins, such as HAVCR2, NT5E, PDCD1, and TIGIT, on control CARMESO from the tumor, whereas IFNγRKO CARMESO exhibited higher CTLA4, ENTPD1, and LAG3 (fig. S14C). Finally, cell profiling revealed a similar expression of type 1 CD4+ helper T cells (Th1), but less regulatory T cells (Treg) in the IFNγRKO CARMESO-treated mice (fig. S14D; left). This further correlated with higher maintenance of CD8+ T cells and cytotoxic cells in the tumors of mice receiving IFNγRKO CARMESO compared to control CARMESO (fig. S14D; middle and right, respectively). Collectively, no major differences in the differentiation, potential exhaustion, and cell types of CAR-T cells with IFNγ-resistance.

We next assessed the expression of apoptosis and cell-death-related genes in CAR-T cells collected from the tumors. In line with our previous observations, control CARMESO exhibited a higher expression of pro-apoptotic genes (Fig. 6F). In contrast, IFNγRKO CARMESO displayed a marked upregulation of anti-apoptotic genes. Compared to resting CAR-T cells (PRE), only CARMESO cells had an increase in interferon-related genes (Fig. 6G). Although both CARMESO and IFNγRKO CARMESO isolated from tumors (POST) displayed an elevation in pro-apoptotic genes compared to CAR-T cells prior to infusion (PRE), CARMESO had a markedly higher pro-apoptotic gene expression profile than that of IFNγRKO CARMESO (Fig. 6H). These findings confirm the in vitro data and suggest that inhibiting the uptake of IFNγ through deletion of IFNγR helps protect CD28 CAR-T cells from cell death.

The data herein show that CAR-T cells consume and are affected by IFNγ, suggesting that CAR-T cells themselves might compete with tumor cells for IFNγ. We hypothesized that deletion of IFNγR on CAR-T cells could increase the exposure of the tumor cells to IFNγ in the microenvironment. Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that interferon-related genes were more highly expressed in the tumors from mice receiving IFNγRKO CARMESO compared to control CARMESO (Fig. 6I). This correlated with a broad upregulation of immune checkpoint proteins, such as CTLA4, ENTPD1 and LAG3, on the tumor compartment (fig. S14E). We further discovered that whereas tumor driver genes, such as IER3 and UBB, were elevated in tumor only and control CARMESO groups, tumors from mice treated with IFNγRKO CARMESO exhibited a higher expression of tumor suppressor genes (fig. S14F,G). In line with the previous data, the upregulation of interferon-related genes in tumors of mice treated with IFNγRKO CARMESO exhibited an increase in pro-apoptotic markers compared to tumor only and CARMESO-treated mice (Fig. 6J–L). Collectively, these data reveal that inhibiting the uptake of IFNγ by CAR-T cells drives greater interferon signaling, and subsequent cell death, in tumor cells. Additionally, the skewing of interferon signaling to the tumor cells correlates with a greater expression of tumor suppressor genes.

### EGFR-targeting IFNγRKO CAR-T cells confer protection from tumor rechallenge

We next sought to determine if IFNγ-resistant CAR-T cells could persist and protect from tumor rechallenge in a different in vivo model. To test this, we generated control CAREGFR and IFNγRKO CAREGFR with an scFv targeting EGFR (Fig. 7A). Since EGFR antigen is more highly expressed on pancreatic tumor cell lines than mesothelin (fig. S14H), EGFR-targeted CAR-T cells can produce more potent responses in this mouse model. Before testing these in vivo, we first confirmed that IFNγRKO CAREGFR exhibited enhanced growth following antigen exposure (fig. S15A) and cytotoxic activity against EGFR+ AsPC-1 tumor cells (fig. S15B).

Mice were treated with EGFR-specific CAR-T cells two weeks after AsPC-1 injection (fig. S15C). In agreement with mesothelin-targeted CAR-T cells, IFNγRKO CAREGFR demonstrated more potent anti-tumor activity compared to CAREGFR (fig. S15D), but no differences in survival (fig. S15E) or CAR-T cell persistence (fig. S15F) were noted.

Additionally, several mice treated with CAREGFR or IFNγRKO CAREGFR exhibited a complete response resulting in no measurable disease in 3/5 mice through day 70 post-CAR-T cell injection. On day 70 after initial CAR-T cell transfer, the cured mice from both the CAREGFR and IFNγRKO CAREGFR groups, plus 5 treatment-naive mice, were injected with AsPC-1 tumor cells and monitored for tumor growth (Fig. 7B). Despite the initial curative response, mice who had originally received control CAREGFR were not protected against a secondary tumor challenge and exhibited tumor growth and survival that was only slightly delayed from the tumor only group (Fig. 7C; fig. S15G,H). On the contrary, IFNγRKO CAREGFR-treated mice exhibited a small tumor relapse upon rechallenge but were able to rapidly clear it and yield long-term curative responses in all mice. This additionally led to longer survival in IFNγRKO CAREGFR-treated mice compared to tumor only and control CAREGFR (Fig. 7D). Overall, these findings confirm that the deletion of IFNγR yields CAR-T cells that can elicit long-term anti-tumor activity and survival. Further, IFNγRKO CAR-T cells demonstrate the ability to protect from tumor rechallenge where control CAR-T cells fail. These data suggest that IFNγ-resistant CAR-T cells have improved expansion and memory formation in vivo.

### IFNγRKO CAR-T cells display increased efficacy and survival in a syngeneic model of triple-negative breast cancer

Our data demonstrate that IFNγRKO CAR-T cells have greater expansion, anti-tumor activity, and survival; however, interpretation of this data is limited due to the lack of an endogenous tumor microenvironment in NSG mice. Since IFNγ can affect multiple cell subsets, including endothelial cells and innate immune cells, we next sought to determine if these phenomena held true in a syngeneic mouse model. To do this, T cells were isolated from CD45.2+ wildtype (WT) or IFNGRKO (IFNγRKO) C57BL/6 mice and retrovirally transduced to express a non-specific control CAR (CARFITC) or a B7H3-targeting CAR (CARB7H3) containing a CD28 costimulatory domain (Fig. 8A; top). The transduction efficiency in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was similar between WT and IFNγRKO T cells (Fig. 8B). Moreover, IFNγRKO CAR-T cells displayed a greater population of central memory T cells in both the CD4+ and CD8+ subsets compared to WT CAR-T cells (Fig. 8C).

To test these CAR-T cells in vivo, we first generated a triple-negative breast cancer cell line that over-expressed the tumor antigen B7H3 (E0771 B7H3) and injected it into the mammary fat pad of CD45.1+ C57BL/6 mice (Fig. 8A; bottom). Tumor-bearing mice were conditioned with cyclophosphamide two days prior to the intravenous administration of 5e6 CD8+ CAR-T cells. Of note, CD4+ CAR-T cells were not injected due to insufficient numbers. As expected, control WT CARFITC, and IFNγRKO CARFITC cells had no effect on tumor growth (Fig. 8D–F). In agreement with the xenograft tumor models, IFNγRKO CARB7H3 displayed greater anti-tumor activity compared to WT CARB7H3. Analysis of the tumor 23 days post-CAR-T cell treatment revealed a higher percentage and number of IFNγRKO CARB7H3 compared to their wildtype counterpart (Fig. 8G). Collectively, these data support our previous findings and demonstrate that IFNγRKO CAR-T cells display increased expansion, persistence, and anti-tumor activity in both immunodeficient and immunocompetent models. We herein report that IFNγ uptake can limit CD28 CAR-T cells by inducing apoptosis and restricting their expansion (fig. S16,). Deletion of IFNγR conferred CD28 CAR-T cells with protection from cell death and increased expansion, and the tumor compartment from IFNγRKO CAR-treated mice displayed greater interferon signaling and cell death.

## DISCUSSION

In this study, we investigated the effects of IFNγ biology on CAR-T cells and demonstrated that IFNγ resistance enhances CAR-T cell engraftment, long-term persistence, and efficacy against hematologic and solid malignancies. Mechanistically, we show that genetic targeting of either IFNγ or IFNγR can protect CD28 CAR-T cells from IFNγ-mediated cell death in vitro and in vivo. Loss of either of these proteins increased persistence without compromising anti-tumor efficacy in models of leukemia and lymphoma. In xenograft solid tumor models, knockout of IFNγR in CAR-T cells resulted in greater tumor control and survival. Furthermore, deletion of IFNγR endowed CAR-T cells functional long-term memory. Finally, we confirmed these results in a syngeneic mouse model, demonstrating that IFNγRKO CAR-T cells exhibit increased expansion in the tumor and anti-tumor efficacy in both immune-competent and -incompetent mouse models.

Due to the risk of tumor relapse, one goal in both hematologic and solid tumors is to generate long-lived memory T cells. Incorporation of costimulatory domains was the first major modification that increased engraftment and persistence of engineered CAR-T cells. Although CAR-T cells containing a CD28 costimulatory domain exhibit potent anti-tumor activity and rapid expansion, they tend to persist for shorter duration relative to CAR-T cells designed with the 4–1BB costimulatory domain (5). This shorter persistence and tendency to lead to T cell exhaustion (28) may limit its clinical efficacy in solid tumors (29), despite its more potent cytotoxic activity in vitro or in the short term (30). Previous studies have explored genetic editing of the CD28 costimulatory domain (31), signal strength (32) and signaling pathway (33) to increase the persistence of these T cells. In our study, we discovered that uptake of IFNγ by CAR-T cells bearing the CD28 signaling domain, but not 4–1BB, limited their durability, in part, through the induction of apoptotic cell death.

The effects of IFNγ signaling in T cells have been studied in the context of TCR signaling, and indicate that although IFNγ can increase the motility and cytotoxicity of CD8+ T cells (15), it also restricts the T cell memory precursor pool (16) and is required for activation-induced cell death (17). Recent studies have further demonstrated that IFNγ signaling in tumor-specific T cells can dampen their anti-tumor activity through inducing cell death (20) and inhibiting the maintenance of stem-like T cells (21). In contrast to TCR-based studies, the effects of IFNγ signaling in the specific context of CAR-T cells are largely unknown. Due to the potent release of IFNγ by CAR-T cells following antigen exposure, the question of how its uptake affects CAR-T cell function is raised. Our data demonstrate that whereas IFNγ has minimal effect on the differentiation, exhaustion, and proliferation of CD28 CAR-T cells in our models, it plays a direct role in the induction of cell death following antigen exposure. Notably, these effects were not observed in CAR-T cells with a 4–1BB costimulatory domain, suggesting that response to IFNγ could differ between clinical CAR-T cell constructs.

Although these findings demonstrate that IFNγ limits CAR-T cell responses, the effects of IFNγ signaling in tumor cells on immunotherapeutic responses are becoming increasingly recognized. Retrospective studies in patients with metastatic melanoma or non-small cell lung cancer have identified the correlation between IFNG and IFNγ-responsive gene signatures with clinical response following treatment with the immune checkpoint inhibitors, pembrolizumab or nivolumab (18, 19). These findings are further supported by preclinical work demonstrating that loss of IFNγR in glioblastoma or pancreatic cancer cells reduces the avidity of CAR-T cells, thereby conferring solid tumors with resistance to CAR-T cell killing (23). These data collectively suggest that whereas IFNγ signaling in the tumor compartment is required for effective immunotherapy, its uptake by T cells might limit their activity. To this end, we discovered that IFNγ-resistant CAR-T cells, capable of producing but not internalizing IFNγ, induced more potent, durable responses in both hematologic and solid malignancies.

In addition to the protection of CAR-T cells from cell death through IFNγR loss, this approach could result in increased exposure of tumor cells to IFNγ. Competition for cytokines (34) and nutrients (35, 36) occurs in the tumor microenvironment and can limit effective T cell responses. Our data suggest that CAR-T cells may compete for IFNγ, thereby limiting the uptake of this cytokine by tumor cells and, potentially, the surrounding tumor microenvironment. Greater interferon uptake in pancreatic tumor cells correlated with increased gene expression of cell death-related markers, as well as a higher expression of tumor suppressor genes. Given the reported potential of IFNγ to skew innate immune cells to an anti-tumorigenic phenotype (9), removing CAR-T cells from competition for IFNγ could not only increase tumor cell death but may potentiate a more favorable tumor microenvironment. It is worth noting that our data herein was primarily focused on the impact of IFNγ on CAR-T cells themselves and do not conclusively prove that CAR-T cells compete for IFNγ in the tumor microenvironment.

Although the increase of interferon signaling in tumor cells reported here correlated with greater cell death gene expression, there was also a widespread upregulation of immune checkpoint proteins, such as CTLA4 and LAG3. Given the role of IFNγ in inducing immune checkpoint proteins (10, 11), this finding is not surprising but highlights the potential for combination with immune checkpoint blockade therapies. As previously mentioned, IFNγ is mechanistically required for effective anti-tumor responses to immune checkpoint therapies (18, 19), but can inhibit the maintenance of intratumoral stem-like T cells (21) and drive the cell death of tumor-specific T cells (20). Thus, IFNγ-resistant CAR-T cells may be better suited for combination with immune checkpoint blockades and other immunotherapies.

A limitation of our study is primarily limiting cell death analysis to markers of apoptosis, which is the primary form of IFNγ-mediated T cell death (17). Since IFNγ can contribute to other forms of cell death, including ferroptosis (25), PANoptosis (26), and pyroptosis (27), it is possible that these pathways may also play a role in tumor immunity interactions. Another limitation is the primary focus on CAR-T cells with a CD28 costimulatory domain, raising the question of how other CAR-T cell products may be affected. Herein, we briefly show that 4–1BB CAR-T cells do not respond to IFNγ like those with a CD28 costimulatory domain contrary to our initial expectations. This is a noteworthy finding as it suggests that although IFNγ is credited with inducing apoptosis in T cells, components of the CAR construct, such as the costimulatory domain, could alter this outcome. A deeper mechanistic understanding of how costimulatory domains alter CAR-T cell responses to IFNγ will be crucial for informing and improving cell products in the clinic. Finally, we reported that IFNγRKO CAR-T cells exhibit greater anti-tumor activity and durability in a syngeneic mouse model; however, the detailed impact of these cells on the surrounding tumor microenvironment is unknown. Though beyond the scope of the current work, future studies will aim to elucidate these effects.

In summary, our data reveals that CD28 IFNγ-resistant CAR-T cells have enhanced anti-tumor efficacy through reduction in CAR-T cell death, enabling enhanced persistence, long-term memory formation, and potentially increasing exposure of tumor cells to IFNγ. These discoveries demonstrate that uptake of IFNγ can limit CAR-T cell responses and that strategic pharmacologic or genetic targeting of this pathway could generate more potent, persistent therapies for patients in the clinic.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Study design.

The objective of the study was to define how IFNγ signaling limits CAR-T cells and leverage gene editing of this pathway to elicit potent, long-term efficacy of CAR-T cells in hematologic and solid malignancies. CRISPR/Cas9 editing was used to generate IFNγ-deficient (IFNγKO) and IFNγ-resistant (IFNγRKO) CAR-T cells, and their phenotype, activation, functionality, cytotoxicity, and proliferation was characterized. Direct effects of IFNγ were further explored using pharmacologic blockade of IFNγ or IFNγR, or introduction of exogenous recombinant human IFNγ. In vitro replicates were variable and are indicated in the figure legends. RNA sequencing of CAR-T cells from both in vitro and in vivo models was used to define genetic changes stemming from loss of IFNγ signaling. Xenograft and syngeneic mouse models of leukemia, lymphoma, pancreatic cancer, and triple-negative breast cancer were evaluated by bioluminescence, caliper measurements, serum collection for detection of IFNγ, and bleeds for CAR-T cell persistence. For in vivo experiments, tumor burden was used to randomize mice into treatment groups.

### Blocking antibodies

Interferon (IFN)-γ signaling was pharmacologically blocked with 20µg/ml Purified NA/LE Mouse Anti-Human IFN-γ Clone NIB42 (BD Biosciences; Cat. No. 551221) or NA/LE Mouse Anti-Human CD119 (IFNγ receptor; IFNγR) Clone GIR-208 (BD Biosciences; Cat. No. 557531). Blocking antibodies were refreshed every 24 hours as needed.

### CAR design and generation

Human anti-CD19 (FMC63 (37)) CAR constructs with either a 4–1BB or CD28 costimulatory domain were synthesized (Genscript) and cloned into a third-generation lentiviral backbone under the regulation of a human EF-1α promoter (22, 23, 38). Additional anti-CD19 constructs were designed to include guide RNA (gRNA) sequences for TRAC (AGAGTCTCTCAGCTGGTACA; CARCD19) with or without gRNAs targeting IFNG (CCAGAGCATCCAAAAGAGTG; IFNγKO CARCD19) or IFNGR1 (GGAGTACCAGATCATGCCAC; IFNγRKO CARCD19). gRNAs were chosen based on previous work (22, 23) and were further used to design anti-mesothelin (SS1 (39)) (CARMESO, IFNγKO CARMESO, IFNγRKO CARMESO) and anti-EGFR (cetuximab (40)) (CAREGFR, IFNγRKO CAREGFR) constructs with a CD28 costimulatory domain. Lentiviral vectors were prepared by transient transfection of 293T cells with packaging and transfer plasmids. Supernatant was harvested at 24- and 48-hours post-transfection, filtered through 45µm filters, and concentrated by ultracentrifugation (20000g for 2 hours at 4°C).

For murine CAR T cells, CAR constructs targeting FITC (control; CARFITC) or the tumor antigen B7H3 (41) (CARB7H3) with an intracellular CD28 costimulatory domain were incorporated into a murine stem cell virus (MSCV) retroviral vector and transfected into Platinum-E cells with packaging and transfer plasmids. Supernatant containing retroviral vectors was collected 72 hours post-transfection, filtered through 45µm filters, and concentrated by ultracentrifugation (20000g for 2 hours at 4°C).

### CAR-T cell production

For human CAR T cell production, peripheral blood of anonymous healthy donor leukapheresis product was purchased from the MGH Blood Bank under an Institutional Review Board-approved protocol and T cells were isolated using the RosetteSep Human T Cell Enrichment Cocktail (STEMCELL Technologies Cat. 15061). T cells were re-suspended in CAR media (RPMI-1640 GlutaMAX + 10% FBS + Pen/Strep (Thermo Scientific Fisher Cat. 15140122) supplemented with 20IU/ml IL-2 (PeproTech Cat. 200–02) and activated using anti-CD3/CD28 Dynabeads (Life Technologies Cat. 40203D) at a ratio of 3 beads for every 1 T cell. Twenty-four hours post-activation, T cells were transduced with one of the lentiviral vectors encoding anti-CD19, -mesothelin or -EGFR CAR constructs described above. Cells were de-beaded five days post-activation and expanded in the presence of 20 IU/ml IL-2. For knockout groups, T cells were re-suspended at 5e6/100µl in Opti-Mem (Thermo Fisher Scientific Cat. 31985088) after de-beading on day 5 and electroporated with 10µg Cas9 mRNA (TriLink Cat. L-7206) at 360V x 001ms. Three to five days later, CD3-T cells were isolated by column purification (EasySep Human APC Positive Selection Kit II; STEMCELL Technologies Cat. 17661) or flow-based cell sorting using the BD FACSAria. Transduction efficiency was determined using mCherry (PE-Texas Red) expression by flow cytometry. Deletion of CD3 (TRAC), IFNγ, and IFNγR was confirmed by flow cytometry. For all functional assays, CAR-T cells were normalized for transduction and isolation efficiency.

To generate murine CAR T cells, T cells were harvested from the spleen and lymph nodes of CD45.2+ C57BL/6 (IMSR_JAX:002014) and Ifngr KO (IMSR_JAX:003288) mice. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were purified by bead-based selection (Miltenyi Biotec) and plated at 5e5 cells/ml in 24-well plates pre-coated with CD3 (2µg/ml) and CD28 (2µg/ml) antibodies in T cell clone medium supplemented with mouse IL-2 (30 IU/ml). T cell clone medium was made using DMEM plus 10% FBS, penicillin/streptomycin (100U/ml), glutamine (2mM), sodium pyruvate (1.5mM), non-essential amino acids (1x, Lonza Cat. 13–114E), vitamins (1x, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. 11120052), arginine (1.16mg/ml), asparagine (36µg/ml), folic acid (14µM),β-mercaptoethanol (57.2mM), and recombinant mouse IL-2 (30U/ml). 24 hours post-activation, fresh concentrated RVs and 8µg/ml of polybrene were added and T cells were spinoculated at 2400rpm for 2 hours at 32°C. 12–14 hours later, fresh T cell clone medium was added. 72 hours post-T cell activation, T cells were moved to uncoated plates for expansion in the presence of murine IL-2 (30 IU/ml). Transduction efficiency was determined using an anti-Myc-Tag (Cell Signaling).

### Cell lines

The human JeKo-1 (CRL-3006), Nalm6 (CRL-3273), AsPC-1 (CRL-1682), BxPC-3 (CRL-1687), and Capan-2 (HTB-80) cell lines were purchased from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Cells were engineered to constitutively express click beetle green luciferase (CBG) and enhanced GFP (GFP) prior to sorting on FACSAria (BD) to obtain a ≥99% CBG-GFP+ population. JeKo-1, Nalm6, AsPC-1, and BxPC-3 cells were cultured in R10 media (RPMI1640 + 10%FBS + penicillin/streptomycin). Capan-2 cells were culture in D10 media (DMEM + 10%FBS + penicillin/streptomycin). All cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma.

The triple-negative breast cancer cell line E0771 (CRL-3461) was purchased from ATCC and transduced with a lentiviral construct encoding murine B7H3 cDNA and a blue fluorescence protein (BFP) reporter cDNA under the EF1α promoter (EF1α-mB7H3-p2a-BFP) to generate a cell line over-expressing mouse B7H3 (E0771 mB7H3 OE).

### Flow cytometry

Cells were stained in the dark for 20 minutes at room temperature in BD Horizon Brilliant Stain Buffer (BD Biosciences) and washed twice with FACS Buffer (PBS + 2% FBS) prior to acquisition. Cells were fixed with Fixation Buffer (BioLegend Cat. 420801) and incubated in Intracellular Staining Permeabilization Wash Buffer (10X) (BioLegend Cat. 421002) with flow antibodies for 30 minutes at room temperature. For functional assessment, CAR-T cells were activated for four hours using Cell Activation Cocktail with Brefeldin A (BioLegend; Cat. 423302) or 18 hours with plate-bound CD19 (Recombinant Human CD19 Fc Chimera Protein, CF; R&D Systems Cat. 9269-CD-050), mesothelin (Recombinant Human Mesothelin; PeproTech Cat. 100–63), or EGFR (Recombinant Human EGF Receptor (EGFR); PeproTech Cat. 100–15R) prior to staining. All antibodies can be found in table S1. Samples were run on a Fortessa X-20 and analyzed using FlowJo software.

### Bead count assay

Cells were stained using the above protocol and then prepared for the bead count assay as follows. CountBright Plus Absolute Counting Beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Cat. C36995) were brought to room temperature, vortexed for 30 seconds, added to samples at 50µl beads/well, and placed on a plate shaker. All samples were run on a Fortessa X-20, analyzed using FlowJo software, and calculations were performed according to Thermo Fisher Scientific protocol.

### Cell death assay

To measure viability, cells were left untreated or activated with plate-bound antigen and stained for flow cytometry using Cleaved Caspase 3 purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (Pacific Blue, Clone D3E9; Cat. 8788S) or Annexin V purchased from BioLegend (APC; Cat. 640920) in Annexin V binding buffer according to protocol (BioLegend Cat. 422201). All samples were kept on ice throughout processing and run on a Fortessa X-20 prior to analysis with FlowJo software.

### Cell trace violet staining and analysis

CAR-T cells were collected (approximately 4e6 CAR+/group), centrifuged and resuspended in 2ml CellTrace Violet Cell Proliferation Kit, for flow cytometry (Thermo Fisher Scientific Cat. C34557) that had been diluted in pre-warmed sterile PBS according to protocol. Cells were incubated at 37°C for 20 minutes and then quenched with 8ml R10 media for 5 minutes at room temperature. Cells were centrifuged, counted, and added to wells with plate-bound antigen or tumor cells as described in figure legends. 1e5 cells were saved and fixed for a day 0 control. Cells were collected 6 days later, and all samples were run on a Fortessa X-20 before analyzing with FlowJo software.

### Analysis of murine peripheral blood samples by flow cytometry

Following the collection of blood from leukemia-, lymphoma-, or pancreatic tumor-bearing NSG mice, samples were processed for flow cytometry. APC-conjugated mouse dump antibodies (Ly-6G/Ly-6C (RB6–8C5), NK1.1 (PK136), CD11b (M1/70), and TER-119/Erythroid cell (TER-119) were added to a FACS tube at 1µl/sample each. 1µl/sample of anti-human CD4 (FITC; SK3; BioLegend) and CD8 (BUV395; RPA-T8; BD Biosciences) antibodies were added to the same tube. The antibody tube was filled to 20µl/sample with PBS and vortexed, then 20µl of mix was carefully added to the bottom of TruCount Tubes (BD Biosciences Cat. 340334). TruCount Tubes were vortexed and incubated in the dark for 10 minutes at room temperature (RT). 50µl of peripheral blood collected from mice was added to corresponding TruCount Tubes, vortexed, and incubated at room temperature in the dark for 10 minutes. BD FACS Lysing Solution 10X Concentrate (BD Biosciences Cat. 349202) was diluted and 450µl was added to each TruCount Tube. Tubes were vortexed and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes prior to running on a Fortessa X-20 and analyzing using FlowJo software.

### phosphoSTAT1 staining

For phosphoflow, cells were resuspended at 1e6/ml and left untreated or given 20ng/ml recombinant human IFNγ (Shenandoah Biotechnology Cat. 100–77) for 20 minutes at 37°C. Cells were fixed at 1:1 ratio with BD Cytofix (BD Biosciences Cat. 554655) for 15 minutes at room temperature. Following centrifugation, cells were resuspended in Perm Buffer III (BD Biosciences Cat. 558050) at 2e6/ml, vortexed vigorously and put on ice for 30 minutes. Cells were stained with PhosphoStat1 Tyr701 (Clone 58D6; Cell Signaling Technology; Cat. 9167) in PBS supplemented with 1% bovine serum albumin (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. A7030) followed by anti-Rabbit IgG (H+L), F(ab’)2 Fragment AF647 (Cell Signaling Technology Cat. 4414). All cells were run on a Fortessa X-20 (BD Biosciences) and analyzed using FlowJo software.

### Incucyte

Donor-derived control, IFNγKO, and IFNγRKO CAR-T cells targeting CD19 were combined with JeKo-1 lymphoma or Nalm6 leukemia cells at a 1:1 effector-to-target ratio and tumor burden (GFP) and proliferation of mCherry+ CAR-T cells was assessed for three days on the Incucyte SX5 (Sartorius). Anti-mesothelin CAR-T cells were cultured at a 1:1 ratio with pancreatic cancer cell lines AsPC-1, BxPC-3, or Capan-2, and tumor burden (GFP) and CAR-T cell proliferation (mCherry) was monitored for 3–5 days. CAR-T cell expansion in response to tumor antigen alone was assessed over a 24-hour period using plate-bound CD19, mesothelin, or EGFR. To measure real-time apoptosis of T cells in response to antigen stimulation, all CAR-T cell groups were added to plates coated with CD19 or mesothelin antigen in the presence of Incucyte Annexin V Dye for Apoptosis - Green according to protocol (Sartorius Cat. 4642) and monitored for 1–3 days.

### Luminex

CAR-T cells were activated with Cell Activation Cocktail without Brefeldin A (BioLegend Cat. 423302) for four hours, or with plate-bound CD19 or mesothelin antigen overnight. Cytokines were measured using the Th1/Th2 Cytokine 11-Plex Human ProcartaPlex Panel according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific Cat. EPX110–10810-901). Samples were run on the FLEXMAP 3D System.

### NanoString

For in vitro studies, CAR-T cells were combined with plate-bound CD19 antigen overnight in the presence or absence of 10ng/ml recombinant human IFNγ. All CAR T cells were lysed using RLT buffer to obtain RNA and code set probes were hybridized with RNA by PCR for 18 hours at 65°C according to NanoString protocol. nCounter gene expression assays (NanoString Technologies) were performed using NanoString XT CAR-T Panel Standard + Customized PLUS panel. Hybridized RNA was loaded into nCounter MAX cartridges, run on the nCounter MAX and quantified using nSolver or nSolver Advanced software. For advanced analysis, donors as covariates was considered. Data are displayed as volcano plots, PCA plots, normalized gene counts, and cell type profiling.

For in vivo studies, 6–10-week-old NSG mice were subcutaneously injected with 1.5e6 AsPC-1 CBG-GFP+ cells (resuspended in 1:1 ratio of sterile PBS and Matrigel (Corning Cat. 356231) 14 days prior to IV administration of 3e6 mesothelin-specific control or IFNγRKO CAR T cells. Mice were euthanized at 14 days post-CAR-T cell infusion and tumors were collected and processed as follows. Each tumor was cut into small pieces using razor blades, treated with digestion media consisting of 10ml warm RPMI (no FBS), 500µl Collagenase P (2mg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich) and 5µl DNase I (50mg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich) and placed in a shaking incubator at 37°C for two hours. Digested tumor samples were filtered through a 70µM filter, then resuspended in cold R10 media (RPMI 1640 + 10% FBS + Pen/Strep). GFP+ tumor cells and mCherry+ CAR-T cells were isolated from digested tumors using a BD FACSAria. Isolated cells were lysed using RLT buffer to obtain RNA and code set probes were hybridized with RNA by PCR for 18 hours at 65°C according to NanoString protocol. nCounter gene expression assays (NanoString Technologies) were performed using NanoString XT CAR-T Panel Standard + Customized PLUS panel (CAR-T) or nCounter PanCancer IO 360 panel (tumor). Hybridized RNA was loaded into nCounter MAX cartridges, run on the nCounter MAX and quantified using nSolver or nSolver Advanced software. For advanced analysis, donors as covariates was considered. Data are displayed as volcano plots, normalized gene counts (heatmaps/scatter plots), and cell type profiling.

### Hematologic malignancy NSG xenograft models

NSG mice (IMSR_JAX:005557) were purchased from Jackson Laboratory and bred under pathogen-free conditions at the MGH Center for Comparative Medicine. 6- to 10-week-old male and female NSG mice were intravenously (IV) injected with 1e6 JeKo-1 or Nalm6 CBG-GFP+ cells. Seven days later, mice were randomized and left untreated (tumor only; TO) or IV injected with 5e5 or 1e6 CAR-T cells and tumor burden was measured by bioluminescence using an Ami spectral imaging apparatus (not blinded) and analyzed with IDL software following intraperitoneal (IP) injection of D-Luciferin substate solution (30mg/ml; Fisher Scientific Cat. PI88294). Mice were bled on days 2 and 14 post-CAR-T injection to monitor IFNγ expression, cytokine profiles, and CAR-T persistence, respectively. In all experiments, bioluminescence was measured weekly. All experiments were performed according to protocols approved by the MGH Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

### Pancreatic cancer NSG xenograft model

NSG mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratory and bred under pathogen-free conditions at the MGH Center for Comparative Medicine. 6- to 10-week-old male or female NSG mice were subcutaneously injected with 1.5e6 AsPC-1 CBG-GFP+ cells (resuspended in 1:1 ratio of sterile PBS and Matrigel 14 days prior to randomization and IV administration of 3e6 mesothelin- or EFGR-targeting CAR-T cells. Only mice with measurable tumors were included. Caliper measurements (not blinded) were conducted weekly to assess tumor burden and CAR-T cell persistence in the blood was assessed at days 7, 14, 21, 28 and 35 post-CAR-T injection. Mice treated with EGFR-specific CAR-T cells that demonstrated curative responses (3/5 KO CAREGFR and 3/5 IFNγRKO CAREGFR) were subcutaneously re-challenged on day 70 with 1.5e6 AsPC-1 tumor cells (1:1 sterile PBS and Matrigel) in the opposing flank to primary tumors and were monitored for tumor growth using weekly caliper measurements. All experiments were performed according to protocols approved by the MGH Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

### Syngeneic triple-negative breast cancer mouse model

6-to 9-week-old C57BL/6 mice, including CD45.2+ (IMSR_JAX:000664), CD45.2+ Ifngr KO (IMSR_JAX:003288), and CD45.1+ (IMSR_JAX:002014), were purchased from Jackson Laboratory. E0771 mB7H3 OE cells (3e5) were injected into the 4th mammary fat pad in a total volume of 100µl of 1:1 PBS/Matrigel solution. Tumor-bearing mice were conditioned with an IV injection of 100µg/g cyclophosphamides on day 2, followed by IV administration of 5e6 CD8+ CAR T cells four days post-tumor implantation. Tumors were measured by caliper (not blinded). 23 days post-CAR-T cell treatment, tumors were collected from mice and dissected by mincing tumor tissue prior to digestion with Collagenase D (2.5mg/ml) for 20 minutes at 37°C. Tumors were then disassociated to single cell suspension by passing tissue through a 70µM filter prior to centrifugation and analysis by flow cytometry. All experiments were performed according to protocols approved by the MGH Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

### Statistical analysis

Individual-level data for all experiments where n<20 are presented in data file S1. All analyses were performed with GraphPad Prism v10 software. Statistical tests and the number of technical or biological replicates are described in each figure legend. Significance for comparisons was determined using unpaired t-test (two groups) or using a one-way or two-way ANOVA (three or more groups) and presented as means ± SEM. For experiments with multiple groups, correction for multiple comparisons was applied (Tukey’s multiple comparisons analysis). Statistical significance for overall survival was measured by log-rank (Mantel-Cox test) for Kaplan-Meier curves. Significance is denoted throughout the paper as P: *<0.05, **>0.01, ***<0.001, ****<0.0001. Statistical tests used, biological/technical replicates, and P values for individual graphs are in the figure legends.
